md_description: This workflow covers the generation of metagenome-assembled genomes from marine microbial communities sampled across ocean depths. Environmental water samples are collected at specified sites and depths, disrupted using chemical and mechanical methods, converted into sequencing libraries, and read on high-throughput sequencing platforms. The resulting sequence data are assembled into metagenome-assembled genomes and evaluated for quality, yielding a dataset suitable for studying microbial genetic makeup and ecological roles in marine ecosystems.

marine_microbial_community_sample.reasoning: This is an Entity node, so I included only intrinsic sample identity, origin, and collection context: where the marine sample came from, how deep it was collected, and the environmental conditions recorded at collection. I excluded processing, sequencing, software, file, and derived-quality fields because those belong to downstream Process, Capture, Signal, and Derivative nodes. I also avoided sample identifiers if they were already generated elsewhere; since no prior fields were provided in already_generated, I used a minimal set centered on collection site, depth, and environmental context rather than operational steps.

md_schema.descr: Name of the oceanic collection site for this marine microbial community sample, recorded at the time of sampling; use a stable site label or station name, for example 'Station A3' or 'North Atlantic transect site 12'.
Latitude of the sampling site in decimal degrees (WGS84), recorded at collection; typical range -90.0 to 90.0, for example 42.3521.
Longitude of the sampling site in decimal degrees (WGS84), recorded at collection; typical range -180.0 to 180.0, for example -61.7834.
Water column depth at which the marine sample was collected, measured in meters at the sampling point; typical range 0 to several thousand meters, for example 50.0, 500.0, or 3000.0.
Broad marine environment where the sample was collected, recorded at collection to distinguish the water column context; examples include surface waters and deep waters.
In situ water temperature at the sampling point, measured during collection and associated with the sample; typical range approximately -2 to 35 Celsius in marine systems, for example 4.2.
In situ salinity of the sampling water at collection, measured as practical salinity units (PSU); typical marine range about 30 to 40 PSU, for example 34.7.
In situ pH of the sampling water at collection, measured at the sampling point; typical marine range approximately 7.5 to 8.5, for example 8.1.
Dissolved oxygen concentration in the sampling water at collection, measured in mg/L; typical marine range varies broadly with depth, for example 2.8 mg/L.
Date on which the marine sample was collected, recorded as the sampling date for the entity; use ISO 8601 date format such as 2026-08-18.

Short description of how the collected marine sample was stored or preserved immediately after collection before downstream processing, for example 'on ice', 'frozen at -80 C', or 'RNAlater preserved'.

chemical_mechanical_lysis.reasoning: This is a Process node, so I included only how the lysis was performed: reagent identity, mechanical disruption mode, protocol conditions, and a process-level outcome/quality indicator. I excluded sample origin, sequencing, files, and downstream assembly/quality metrics because those belong to Entity, Capture, Signal, and Derivative nodes respectively. I also avoided repeating entity fields like site, depth, or environmental conditions from the marine sample. No prior generated fields were supplied in this turn, so I did not have to suppress overlaps beyond staying within process territory.

md_schema.descr: Name of the chemical reagent used to chemically disrupt cells during the lysis step, recorded at the process stage; use a reagent name or mixture label such as 'SDS', 'lysozyme', or 'CTAB buffer'.

Concentration of the primary lysis reagent used in the chemical disruption step, measured at the time of preparation; report in the units used by the protocol, commonly mg/mL, percent weight/volume, or mmol/L, for example 10 mg/mL or 2% w/v.
Mechanical cell disruption method applied during lysis, recorded as the active disruption technique used on the marine sample; examples include bead beating, vortexing with beads, or homogenization.
Duration of the mechanical disruption phase, measured from the start to the end of active disruption for the lysis step; typical range is seconds to tens of minutes, for example 60 to 900 seconds.

Instrument or device intensity setting used for mechanical disruption, recorded at the process stage as the active operating level; use the native device scale or a normalized setting, for example 'high', '5.0 m/s', or 'setting 7'.
Temperature at which the chemical and mechanical lysis reaction was carried out, measured during the process step; typical range approximately 0 to 65 Celsius, for example 4.0 or 37.0.
Total elapsed time for the combined chemical and mechanical lysis step, measured from reagent addition to completion; typical range is a few minutes to several hours, for example 30.0.

Total volume of lysis buffer or reagent mixture applied to the sample during the process step, measured at setup or immediately before disruption; typical range tens to hundreds of microliters, for example 200.0.

Process-level indicator of lysis success or nucleic-acid release after disruption, recorded immediately after the lysis step; examples include visual turbidity change, DNA release note, or a simple pass/fail assessment.

lysed_marine_sample.reasoning: This is an Entity node, so I included only intrinsic properties of the lysed sample itself: that it resulted from lysis, what material is now present, and whether the material is suitable for downstream library construction. I excluded the lysis protocol parameters because those belong to the upstream Process node, and I excluded library preparation, sequencing, and computed quality fields because those belong downstream. No already_generated list was provided in this turn, so I kept the schema limited to non-overlapping entity descriptors rather than any processing or measurement fields.

md_schema.descr: Identifier of the upstream marine microbial community sample from which this lysed sample was derived; use the original sample identifier format established at the root entity level, for example 'SMP_000123'.

Current physical state of the entity after disruption, recorded as the sample material status at the handoff to downstream library construction; describe whether it is a crude lysate, clarified lysate, or pellet-plus-supernatant mixture.
Whether nucleic acids were successfully released and are present in the lysed sample at the time it is passed to library preparation; record as a yes/no status based on the post-lysis sample check.
Storage or holding condition of the lysed sample before downstream library preparation, recorded for the entity handoff; examples include 'on ice', '4 C short-term', or 'frozen at -20 C'.

Whether the lysed sample was considered suitable for downstream library construction at the time of transfer; this is a sample-status property, not a protocol parameter, and is typically recorded as a pass/fail-style compatibility flag.

library_preparation.reasoning: This is a Process node, so I included only the library construction workflow itself: input nucleic-acid handling, adapter/index strategy, amplification, size-selection, and a process-level success indicator. I excluded sample-origin fields, sequencing platform configuration, raw file outputs, and assembly/quality results because those belong to Entity, Capture, Signal, and Derivative nodes. No already_generated list was provided in this turn, so I focused on process-specific parameters that a downstream user would need to reproduce library preparation without duplicating entity or output metadata.

md_schema.descr: Type of released nucleic acid used as input to library preparation, recorded at the start of the process; examples include DNA, metagenomic DNA, or DNA-enriched lysate.

Name of the library preparation kit or protocol used to convert nucleic acids into sequencing-ready libraries, recorded at the process stage; use the commercial kit or in-house protocol label, for example 'Nextera XT' or 'Ligation-based metagenomic prep'.

Adapter or indexing strategy used during library construction, recorded as the process design choice that makes the library sequencing-ready; examples include tagmentation adapters, ligation adapters, single-index, or dual-index indexing.
Number of PCR cycles used during library amplification, measured as the count of thermal cycling rounds applied in the library preparation step; typical range is 0 to 20 cycles, for example 8.
Target fragment insert size for the prepared sequencing library, specified during library construction and usually measured in base pairs; typical range is about 100 to 1000 bp, for example 350 bp.
Method used to select or enrich the desired library fragment size range during preparation, recorded at the process stage; examples include bead-based selection, gel extraction, or none.
Mass of nucleic acid input used to start library preparation, measured immediately before the protocol begins; typical range is sub-ng to hundreds of ng, for example 50 ng.

Process-level indicator of whether the library preparation produced a sequencing-ready library that passed the internal check at the end of the step; record as a simple outcome flag, not a file or sequencing quality metric.

sequencing_library.reasoning: This is an Entity node, so I included intrinsic properties of the prepared sequencing library itself: library identity, design characteristics, and physical composition/size that remain true after preparation. I excluded library-preparation parameters because those belong to the upstream Process node, and I excluded sequencing instrument settings and read/file properties because those belong to downstream Capture and Signal nodes. No already_generated list was provided, so I avoided repeating generic sample identifiers and focused on library-specific descriptors needed to recognize and reuse the prepared metagenomic library.

md_schema.descr: Unique identifier for the prepared metagenomic sequencing library entity, using the dataset's library naming convention such as 'LIB_0001' or a barcode-derived ID.
Identifier of the marine microbial community sample from which this sequencing library was derived; use the upstream sample identifier format, for example 'SMP_000123'.

Broad library class describing the prepared entity at the handoff to sequencing; for this workflow it should identify a metagenomic sequencing library rather than an amplicon or transcriptomic library.
Whether the library preserves strand information, recorded as an intrinsic library attribute at completion of preparation; many metagenomic DNA libraries are unstranded.
Indexing or barcode scheme embedded in the library entity for multiplexing, recorded as the library is finalized; examples include single index, dual index, or sample barcode identifiers.
Average fragment size of the prepared sequencing library, measured in base pairs after size selection and before sequencing; typical range is about 100 to 1000 bp, for example 350 bp.
Concentration of the finalized sequencing library, measured before loading onto the sequencing platform; typical range is sub-ng/µL to tens of ng/µL, for example 4.8 ng/µL.
Overall intrinsic status of the prepared library at release to sequencing, recorded as a simple categorical assessment such as pass or needs_rework based on internal QC checks.

high_throughput_sequencing.reasoning: This is a Capture node, so I included only the measurement session and instrument configuration: platform identity, manufacturer/model/serial information, run chemistry, read setup, loading and runtime settings, and capture-session QC. I excluded library intrinsic properties, raw file format/path/size, and downstream assembly metrics because those belong to Entity, Signal, and Derivative nodes. I also avoided repeating any sample or library identifiers already established upstream. The schema is focused on what the operator actively configured or verified on the sequencer, which is the semantic territory of Capture.

md_schema.descr: Human-readable name of the sequencing instrument used for this capture session, recorded at run setup; examples include 'Illumina NovaSeq 6000', 'PacBio Sequel IIe', or 'Oxford Nanopore PromethION'.
Manufacturer of the sequencing instrument, recorded as part of the capture hardware description at run setup; examples include Illumina, PacBio, or Oxford Nanopore Technologies.
Instrument model used for the sequencing capture session, recorded at setup; for example 'NovaSeq 6000', 'Sequel IIe', or 'PromethION 24'.
Serial number of the sequencing instrument used for this run, recorded for traceability at capture setup; use the instrument's manufacturer-assigned serial string, for example 'SN12345678'.
Sequencing chemistry or reagent kit version selected for the run, recorded at capture setup because it controls the instrument chemistry and read generation behavior; for example 'v1.5' or 'HiFi v3'.
Type of flow cell or sequencing consumable loaded for the capture session, recorded before the run begins; examples include 'S4', '8M SMRT Cell', or 'R10.4.1'.
Target read length configured for the sequencing run, measured in base pairs and set before acquisition; typical range varies by platform, for example 150 bp, 250 bp, or 10000 bp.
Run mode or acquisition profile selected on the instrument, recorded at setup to define how reads are generated; examples include rapid, high-output, or long-read mode.

Concentration of the library loaded onto the instrument for the sequencing session, measured immediately before run initiation; report in pM for short-read platforms or an equivalent platform-specific loading unit, for example 10.0 pM.
Total duration of the sequencing capture session, measured from run start to run completion; typical range is hours to days, for example 24.0 or 72.0.

Overall end-of-run capture quality status recorded immediately after sequencing completes, summarizing whether the instrument session met internal expectations; examples include pass, warning, or fail.

raw_sequence_reads.reasoning: This is a Signal node, so I included only properties of the raw data artefact itself: file format, storage, size, read counts, base-call dimensions, and technical file-level quality indicators. I excluded sequencing instrument settings and library properties because those belong to the upstream Capture and Entity nodes, and I excluded preprocessing/assembly metrics because those belong downstream. No already_generated list was provided in this turn, so I chose read-output descriptors that a downstream user would need to locate, validate, and use the FASTQ files without repeating capture configuration.

md_schema.descr: File format of the raw sequencing output produced by the instrument, recorded as the artefact format at the time of data export; for this workflow it is typically FASTQ, including compressed variants if used.
File name of the raw reads artefact as stored in the dataset or object repository, recorded for traceability of the Signal node; example names include 'sample01_R1.fastq.gz' or 'runA_merged.fastq'.

Storage location or relative path to the raw sequence file at the time of metadata capture, recorded so the raw data artefact can be located; examples include a shared filesystem path or object-store URI.
Size of the raw sequence reads file in bytes, measured on the stored artefact after acquisition and export; typical range spans megabytes to terabytes, for example 4587321992.
Total number of called bases represented in the raw sequencing output, measured from the raw FASTQ artefact; typical values depend on platform and run depth, for example 1.2e10 bases.
Number of raw reads or sequences present in the FASTQ artefact, counted from the file after generation; for paired-end data this may be recorded per file or per merged artefact, for example 25000000.
Average read length in base pairs computed directly from the raw sequencing file, recorded as a file-level technical summary; typical range depends on platform, for example 150 bp or 10000 bp.

Technical quality flag for the raw sequence file itself, recorded from file validation or run export checks; examples include pass, warning, or fail, and it refers to data integrity rather than biological interpretation.
Optional checksum or content hash for the raw sequence file, recorded to verify file integrity during transfer or storage; use a reproducible string such as an MD5 or SHA256 hash.

read_processing.reasoning: This is a Process node, so I included only the preprocessing operations applied to the reads and the process-level outcome. I covered trimming, filtering, deduplication, host/contaminant removal, and normalization because those are the core actions of read cleaning before assembly. I excluded raw file properties because those belong to the upstream Signal node, and I excluded processed-read file properties because they belong to the downstream Signal node. I also avoided assembly, capture, and sample-origin fields to stay within process territory.

md_schema.descr: Name of the software or pipeline used to clean or standardize sequencing reads before assembly, recorded at the process stage; examples include 'fastp', 'Trimmomatic', 'BBTools', or a custom workflow name.
Version of the read-processing software used for this preprocessing step, recorded to reproduce the exact cleaning behavior; examples include '0.23.4' or 'v1.2.0'.

Repository, package source, or code location for the read-processing software or workflow, recorded as the process implementation reference; examples include a GitHub URL, conda package name, or container registry reference.
Whether sequencing adapters were removed during preprocessing of the raw reads, recorded as a process parameter at the time reads were cleaned.
Minimum Phred quality score threshold used for trimming low-quality read ends or bases during preprocessing; typical values are 10 to 30, for example 20.
Minimum read length retained after preprocessing, measured in base pairs and enforced during filtering; typical values are 20 to several hundred bp, for example 50 bp.

Method used to remove contaminant or non-target sequences during preprocessing, recorded as the active filtering approach; examples include host-mapping, reference-based filtering, or k-mer screening.
Whether paired-end reads were merged during preprocessing, recorded as a process choice when the workflow combines overlapping read pairs prior to assembly.
Whether duplicate reads were removed during preprocessing, recorded as a process parameter for read standardization before assembly.
Fraction of raw reads retained after preprocessing, calculated at the end of the process as a simple yield indicator; for example 0.72 means 72 percent of input reads passed filtering.

processed_reads.reasoning: This is a Signal node, so I included only properties of the processed read artefact: file identity, format, size, read counts, length summaries, normalization state, and file-level QC. I excluded the upstream read-processing parameters and software because those belong to the Process node, and I excluded assembly inputs/outputs because those belong downstream. I also avoided repeating raw-read file metadata except where needed to describe the processed artefact itself, keeping the schema focused on the cleaned read file that is ready for assembly.

md_schema.descr: File name of the processed reads artefact stored after preprocessing, recorded as the technical identifier for this Signal node; example names include 'sample01_clean.fastq.gz' or 'sample01_filtered_R1.fastq.gz'.

Storage path or URI of the processed reads file at the time of metadata capture, recorded so the cleaned read artefact can be located for assembly; examples include a filesystem path or object-store URI.
File format of the processed reads artefact after cleaning or normalization, recorded as the stored data format; for this workflow it is typically FASTQ or a compressed FASTQ variant.
Size of the processed reads file in bytes, measured on the stored artefact after preprocessing; typical range is megabytes to terabytes depending on run depth, for example 1287321992.
Number of reads remaining in the processed artefact after filtering or normalization, counted directly from the file; for example 18000000.
Total number of bases retained in the processed reads artefact, measured from the cleaned file; this is a file-level summary useful for assembly input characterization, for example 2.7e9 bases.
Average read length in base pairs computed from the processed reads file, recorded after trimming and filtering; typical range depends on platform, for example 140 bp or 9500 bp.

Whether the processed reads were normalized in abundance or coverage before assembly, recorded as an artefact property of the Signal node; use this only when normalization is reflected in the stored file.
Technical quality flag for the processed reads artefact after preprocessing and export, recorded as a file-level check outcome; examples include pass, warning, or fail.
Checksum or content hash of the processed reads file, recorded for integrity verification during storage or transfer; use a reproducible string such as an MD5 or SHA256 hash.

genome_assembly.reasoning: This is a Process node, so I included only the assembly operation itself: software identity, version, repository, algorithmic settings, and process-level output quality. I excluded processed-read file properties because those belong to the upstream Signal node, and I excluded contig/MAG file properties because those belong to the downstream Derivative node. I also avoided quality-assessment metrics like completeness or contamination because those are explicitly owned by the separate quality_assessment process and mag_quality_metrics derivative. No already_generated list was provided in this turn, so I focused on assembly parameters that are necessary to reproduce the reconstruction step without describing the output artefacts.

md_schema.descr: Name of the genome assembly software used to reconstruct contigs and MAGs from processed reads, recorded at the process stage; examples include 'metaSPAdes', 'MEGAHIT', or 'Flye'.
Version of the assembly software used for this reconstruction step, recorded for reproducibility of the exact algorithmic behavior; examples include 'v1.2.9' or '3.15.0'.
Repository, distribution source, or code location for the assembly software, recorded as the process implementation reference; examples include a GitHub URL, package name, or container reference.

K-mer sizes used by the assembler during reconstruction, recorded as the algorithmic parameter set for the process; provide one or more values such as 21,33,55 or a software-specific default description.

Minimum contig length threshold used by the assembler or post-assembly filtering within the assembly process, measured in base pairs; typical values range from a few hundred to several thousand bp, for example 1000 bp.
Assembly mode or strategy selected for the process, recorded as the active reconstruction setting; examples include metagenomic, single-sample, coassembly, or long-read mode.
Memory limit or requested memory allocation used to run the assembly process, measured in gigabytes and recorded for reproducibility of the computational environment; for example 256.0.
Number of CPU threads used by the assembly software during the reconstruction process, recorded as a computational setting; typical values are 1 to 256, for example 32.
Process-level indicator of whether the assembly run completed successfully and produced usable contigs, recorded immediately at the end of the assembly step; examples include pass, partial, or fail.

assembled_mag_contigs.reasoning: This is a Derivative node, so I included only computed output properties of the assembled contigs/MAGs: file identity, format, dimensions, contig statistics, and derived technical quality indicators. I excluded assembly software settings and algorithmic parameters because those belong to the upstream Process node, and I excluded quality-assessment completeness/contamination metrics because those are assigned to the separate quality_assessment process and mag_quality_metrics derivative. I also avoided raw or processed read properties since they are upstream Signal nodes. The schema focuses on what the derived MAG contig dataset is, how large it is, and how to use it downstream.

md_schema.descr: File name of the computed contig or MAG output artefact, recorded as the derivative dataset identifier; example names include 'sample01_assembly.fasta' or 'MAG_set_001.fna'.

Storage path or URI of the assembled contig artefact at the time of metadata capture, recorded so the derived output can be located for downstream analysis; examples include a filesystem path or object-store URI.
File format of the assembled MAG contigs output, recorded as the computed artefact format; for genome assemblies this is typically FASTA or a compressed FASTA variant.
Size of the assembled contigs file in bytes, measured on the stored derivative artefact; typical range is megabytes to gigabytes, for example 53217822.
Number of contigs present in the assembled MAG output, counted directly from the derivative file; for example 482.
Total number of assembled bases represented in the contig set, measured from the derivative artefact; typical range varies by sample depth and assembly success, for example 2.8e8 bases.
N50 contig length of the assembled MAG output, calculated from the derivative contig set in base pairs; typical values range from a few hundred to many thousands bp, for example 14500 bp.
Length of the longest contig in the assembled output, measured in base pairs from the derivative file; for example 182300 bp.
Fraction of ambiguous bases (for example Ns) present in the assembled contigs file, calculated from the derivative artefact as a technical assembly quality indicator; values range from 0.0 to 1.0.

Overall derivative status of the assembled MAG output, recorded after computation to indicate whether the contig set is usable for downstream quality assessment; examples include pass, warning, or fail.

quality_assessment.reasoning: This is a Process node, so I included only the quality-assessment operation: software identity, version, repository, metric thresholds, and process-level result. I excluded assembly output file properties because those belong to the upstream Derivative node, and I excluded the computed quality metrics themselves because those belong to the downstream mag_quality_metrics Derivative node. I also avoided capture, signal, and entity territory. The schema captures what was done to evaluate the assemblies and the criteria used to classify them, without repeating the metric outputs.

md_schema.descr: Name of the software or pipeline used to evaluate MAG quality, recorded at the process stage; examples include 'CheckM', 'QUAST', or a custom quality-control workflow.
Version of the quality-assessment software used for this step, recorded for reproducibility of the exact evaluation behavior; examples include '1.2.3' or 'v5.0.2'.

Repository, package source, or code location for the quality-assessment software, recorded as the process implementation reference; examples include a GitHub URL, conda package name, or container reference.
Completeness percentage threshold used to classify assembled MAGs during quality assessment, measured or set at the process stage; common thresholds are around 50 to 90 percent, for example 90.0.
Contamination percentage threshold used to classify assembled MAGs during quality assessment, measured or set at the process stage; common thresholds are around 0 to 10 percent, for example 5.0.

Classification scheme applied to the MAGs during quality assessment, recorded as the rule set used to label outputs; examples include 'high_quality_medium_quality_low_quality' or a custom project scheme.
Number of CPU threads used by the quality-assessment software during evaluation, recorded as a computational setting for reproducibility; typical values are 1 to 64, for example 8.
Total runtime of the quality-assessment process, measured from start to completion of the evaluation; typical range is minutes to hours, for example 12.5.

Process-level outcome flag indicating whether the MAG quality assessment completed successfully and produced usable classifications, recorded immediately after the step ends; examples include pass, warning, or fail.

mag_quality_metrics.reasoning: This is a Derivative node, so I included only the computed quality metrics and their file/result properties: completeness, contamination, strain heterogeneity, scoring, classification, and derived output location. I excluded the quality-assessment software and thresholds because those belong to the upstream Process node, and I excluded contig/assembly properties because those belong to the upstream Derivative node for assembled MAG contigs. I also avoided sample, capture, and signal territory. The schema is focused on the actual computed MAG quality results that downstream users will filter, rank, or curate on.

md_schema.descr: File name or table name of the derived MAG quality metrics output, recorded as the artefact identifier for this derivative dataset; example names include 'mag_qc.tsv' or 'checkm_results.csv'.

Storage path or URI of the derived MAG quality metrics artefact, recorded so the quality results can be located for downstream curation and filtering; examples include a filesystem path or object-store URI.
Computed genome completeness percentage for the assembled MAG, derived from the quality assessment and measured as a percent; typical values range from 0 to 100, for example 92.4.
Computed contamination percentage for the assembled MAG, derived from the quality assessment and measured as a percent; typical values range from 0 to 100, for example 3.1.
Computed strain heterogeneity percentage for the assembled MAG, if estimated by the quality tool, recorded as a percent; typical values range from 0 to 100, for example 7.8.

Composite quality score assigned to the MAG from the derived assessment results, recorded as the computed ranking or summary metric used for prioritization; the exact scale should follow the pipeline definition, for example 0.0 to 1.0 or 0 to 100.

Derived quality class assigned to the MAG based on completeness and contamination metrics, recorded as the downstream classification used for curation decisions; examples include high quality, medium quality, and low quality.
Overall derived pass/fail flag for the MAG based on the computed quality metrics, recorded as the final filter outcome used by the workflow; examples include pass, warning, or fail.
Number of marker genes recovered in the MAG as reported by the quality assessment output, recorded as a derived count useful for comparing genome recovery across bins; for example 104.

mag_curation_and_annotation.reasoning: This is a Process node, so I included only the curation/annotation operation itself: annotation software identity, version, repository, curation criteria, and process-level outcome. I excluded assembled contig properties and MAG quality metrics because those belong to upstream Derivative nodes, and I excluded the final curated dataset file properties because those belong to the downstream Derivative node. I also avoided sample, capture, and raw signal territory. The fields are aimed at what was actively done to curate and annotate the MAGs, not the resulting annotated dataset contents.

md_schema.descr: Name of the software or pipeline used to curate and annotate the assembled MAGs, recorded at the process stage; examples include 'Prokka', 'DRAM', 'Bakta', or a custom annotation workflow.
Version of the curation and annotation software used for this step, recorded for reproducibility of the exact annotation behavior; examples include '1.14.6' or 'v1.5.0'.

Repository, package source, or code location for the curation/annotation software or workflow, recorded as the process implementation reference; examples include a GitHub URL, conda package name, or container reference.
Name of the reference database used for functional or taxonomic annotation during curation, recorded at the process stage; examples include KEGG, GTDB, Pfam, eggNOG, or NCBI RefSeq.
Version or release date of the annotation database used in curation, recorded so annotations can be reproduced against the same reference set; examples include '2024-04' or 'v5.0'.

High-level rules used to select, merge, or filter MAGs during curation, recorded as the decision logic for producing the final interpretive dataset; examples include keeping only high-quality MAGs or removing bins below a contamination threshold.
Highest taxonomic level targeted or reported during annotation, recorded as a process choice for the interpretive dataset; examples include domain, phylum, class, genus, or species.
Whether functional annotation was performed as part of the curation step, recorded as a process-level choice before producing the final dataset.

Process-level outcome flag indicating whether the curation and annotation step completed successfully and produced a usable final dataset, recorded at process completion; examples include pass, warning, or fail.

curated_mag_dataset.reasoning: This is a Derivative node, so I included only properties of the final interpreted dataset: dataset identity, file/storage characteristics, composition, annotation coverage, and derived usability/quality indicators. I excluded curation and annotation software parameters because those belong to the upstream Process node, and I excluded raw assembly and MAG quality metrics because those belong to upstream Derivative nodes. I also avoided sample, capture, and signal territory. The fields below describe the final curated MAG dataset itself and the information downstream users need to locate, trust, and reuse it.

md_schema.descr: Human-readable name of the final curated MAG dataset, recorded as the derivative dataset identifier; use the project naming convention such as 'Marine_MAG_curated_set_v1'.
Primary file name of the final curated and annotated MAG dataset artefact, recorded as the dataset file identifier; example names include 'curated_mag_dataset.tsv' or 'marine_mags_annotated.fna'.

Storage path or URI of the final curated dataset artefact, recorded so the interpretive dataset can be located for downstream ecological and genetic analysis; examples include a filesystem path or object-store URI.
File format or table format of the curated MAG dataset, recorded as the final derivative artefact format; examples include TSV, CSV, FASTA, GFF, JSON, or a multi-file package.

Size of the final curated dataset artefact in bytes, measured on the stored derivative file or package; typical range is kilobytes to gigabytes depending on included sequences and annotations, for example 24578122.
Number of curated MAGs included in the final dataset, counted after curation and annotation are complete; for example 128.
Fraction of curated MAGs or genes that received at least one annotation in the final dataset, calculated from the derivative outputs; values range from 0.0 to 1.0, for example 0.87.
Fraction of curated MAGs that received a taxonomic assignment in the final dataset, calculated from the annotated outputs; values range from 0.0 to 1.0, for example 0.95.

Overall technical and interpretive usability flag for the curated MAG dataset, recorded after curation and annotation to indicate whether it is ready for downstream ecological and genetic analysis; examples include pass, warning, or fail.
Release version of the final curated MAG dataset, recorded as the version label used for distribution and reuse; examples include 'v1.0', 'v2.1', or a date-based release tag.
